What does "the aquifer, rather than the meter, imposes a limit" mean in the passage?  
Read the following passage carefully and answer the five questions that follow by selecting your answers based solely on the content of the passage and the opinion of the author only. India's groundwater economy rests on a paradox. The electricity that lifts water from beneath the ground is among the most heavily subsidised inputs in Indian agriculture; and precisely because that power is nearly free at the margin, pumping continues until the aquifer, rather than the meter, imposes a limit. Successive attempts to price farm power have foundered on political resistance, and metering, where it exists, is often honoured in the breach. An alternative approach inverts the incentive rather than raising the price. Under the solar irrigation cooperative model piloted in Gujarat, a group of farmers was given grid-connected solar pumps together with a guaranteed buy-back tariff for whatever surplus power they exported to the utility. Sunshine, and not diesel or subsidised grid supply, now drives the pump. Every unit of electricity that is not spent on pumping becomes a unit that can be sold. Water saved is thereby converted into income earned, and the cultivator acquires a direct financial stake in his own restraint. The cooperative form was not incidental to the design. An individual farmer negotiating alone with a distribution utility would have found the paperwork forbidding and his bargaining position negligible. Aggregation reduced transaction costs, secured a common tariff, and gave smallholders a standing they could not have commanded singly. Critics are not silenced by these results. They point out that the buy-back tariff is itself a subsidy, merely relocated from the electricity bill to the procurement price. More seriously, a solar pump, once installed, costs almost nothing to run; if the buy-back price is set too low, the incentive to conserve collapses and the pump becomes an instrument of extraction rather than of restraint. The design of the tariff, not the sophistication of the technology, is therefore the crux of the matter. The experiment has since informed the decentralised-generation component of national programmes. Whether it travels well — to regions of different aquifer behaviour, smaller holdings and thirstier cropping patterns — remains, on the evidence so far, an open question.
options: Meters are rarely installed correctly on agricultural connections.
Pumping is checked by the physical exhaustion of water and not by its cost.
Farmers prefer to measure water drawn rather than power consumed.
Electricity to farms is supplied only for limited hours each day.

questions.question: Which one of the following best states the author's objection to calling the model subsidy-free? Read the following passage carefully and answer the five questions that follow by selecting your answers based solely on the content of the passage and the opinion of the author only. India's groundwater economy rests on a paradox. The electricity that lifts water from beneath the ground is among the most heavily subsidised inputs in Indian agriculture; and precisely because that power is nearly free at the margin, pumping continues until the aquifer, rather than the meter, imposes a limit. Successive attempts to price farm power have foundered on political resistance, and metering, where it exists, is often honoured in the breach. An alternative approach inverts the incentive rather than raising the price. Under the solar irrigation cooperative model piloted in Gujarat, a group of farmers was given grid-connected solar pumps together with a guaranteed buy-back tariff for whatever surplus power they exported to the utility. Sunshine, and not diesel or subsidised grid supply, now drives the pump. Every unit of electricity that is not spent on pumping becomes a unit that can be sold. Water saved is thereby converted into income earned, and the cultivator acquires a direct financial stake in his own restraint. The cooperative form was not incidental to the design. An individual farmer negotiating alone with a distribution utility would have found the paperwork forbidding and his bargaining position negligible. Aggregation reduced transaction costs, secured a common tariff, and gave smallholders a standing they could not have commanded singly. Critics are not silenced by these results. They point out that the buy-back tariff is itself a subsidy, merely relocated from the electricity bill to the procurement price. More seriously, a solar pump, once installed, costs almost nothing to run; if the buy-back price is set too low, the incentive to conserve collapses and the pump becomes an instrument of extraction rather than of restraint. The design of the tariff, not the sophistication of the technology, is therefore the crux of the matter. The experiment has since informed the decentralised-generation component of national programmes. Whether it travels well — to regions of different aquifer behaviour, smaller holdings and thirstier cropping patterns — remains, on the evidence so far, an open question.
options: The pumps themselves were supplied at public expense.
The support has been shifted from the power bill to the price paid for surplus power.
Cooperatives receive preferential treatment from the utility.
Metering of farm connections continues to be waived.

questions.question: What is the primary concern raised by the passage regarding the psychological effects of social media on teenagers? Read the following passage and answer the questions based on it: Research on the psychological consequences of social media on teenagers is complex and becoming more urgent, raising important issues regarding corporate responsibility and cognitive development. The ubiquitous presence of platforms designed to maximise interaction has led many to wonder whether they are reengineering the brains of adolescents, essentially changing the way they think and feel about the world. The relentless, dopamine-reinforced cycles of likes, shares, and notifications habituate the teen brain for instant rewards, possibly lowering the ability for delayed reward and focused, in-depth attention. Also, the edited and sometimes idealised character of online material creates a culture of constant social comparison, resulting in increased rates of anxiety, depression, and body dysmorphic concerns. The pressure to express an idealised digital self and the anxiety about missing out (FOMO) result in a constant state of social and emotional monitoring that can be harmful to a healthy sense of worth and identity development. This irrefutable psychological burden puts the question of accountability in the spotlight. Critics are saying that social media companies, by deliberately creating addictive algorithms and profiting from the very engagement that is hurting people, have both moral and ethical responsibility to safeguard their youngest users. They are saying that the platforms' inaction regarding strong age verification, content blocking, and responsible limits on usage amounts to a dereliction of responsibility, much like other industries are responsible for the effects of their products. On the other hand, platforms and their allies tend to cite the importance of parental control and personal agency, claiming that it is hard to create a direct causal relationship between platform usage and particular mental health effects. Yet, the scale of the problem and the powerful anecdotal and nascent empirical evidence encourage an appraisal of the issue at a more systematic level. In the end, it's not a matter of blaming one thing, but rather finding a collective paradigm of responsibility involving increased government oversight, an inherent change in corporate values towards users' welfare, and enhanced digital literacy and critical thinking education among young people themselves.
options: Social media fosters stronger relationships in teens
Social media contributes to improved cognitive development
Social media alters the way teens think and feel about the world
Social media platforms provide healthier forms of interaction
